newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels swap proposals to end hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels swap proposals to end hostage crisis.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 men captive exchanged proposals on Wednesday for bloodlessly ending the 78-day Lima hostage crisis and agreed to meet again on Friday.

But mediators in face-to-face talks between government negotiators and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas holed up in the Japanese ambassador's home did not reveal the contents of those proposals.

"Both sides have concluded the presentation of proposals and have responded to various questions put forward by the commission of guarantors in order to clarify some points," said Anthony Vincent, Canada's ambassador to Peru and a guarantor.
He did not give more details of the proposals.
Reading from a statement, Vincent told reporters that the commission "will examine both proposals with the objective of facilitating the continuation of the discussions."

He added that Wednesday's two-hour meeting between government negotiators Domingo Palermo and Jose Antonio Payet and MRTA chief Nestor Cerpa and his No. 2 Rolly Rojas took place "in an atmosphere of cordiality."

Shortly after the meeting, a partial blackout in the area around the diplomatic compound left news photographers and cameramen in three buildings overlooking the mansion in the dark. It was unclear what caused the power failure.

The meeting was the ninth since Feb. 11, when talks aimed at setting an agenda for definitive negotiations to resolve the crisis were restarted. No time was given for the start of Friday's 10th round.
Wednesday's meeting held the prospect of the start of real bargaining after President Alberto Fujimori said on Tuesday that the government planned to present an "all-inclusive proposal" to the MRTA.
But the round of talks began amid pessimism about a quick end to the ordeal after rebels poured water on plans to lure them out with an offer of asylum abroad.

Cerpa served notice on Tuesday the guerrillas were holding firm to their chief demand -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- and would not simply accept the government's offers of safe passage to Cuba.
That defiant stance was underscored just before Wednesday's meeting got under way.

As the MRTA leaders were driven in a Red Cross sedan to a safe house across the street from the besieged residence, their comrades in the mansion defiantly sang a ballad about a bloody battle with security forces. They then yelled: "Nobody is surrendering here, damn it!"

While the proposals were kept secret, opposition daily La Republica cited on Wednesday official sources saying the government's plan would include guarantees it will not seek to extradite the rebels if they fly to asylum.

Although the government would stand by its refusal to free any prisoners, the proposal does not rule out the possibility that Fujimori might eventually grant amnesties to MRTA members, the paper reported.
Fujimori has hinted at other concessions to end Latin America's longest hostage siege, possibly a softening of harsh conditions for MRTA prisoners and reform of trial processes.

But in a statement sent to Reuters via electronic-mail early on Wednesday, the MRTA repeated its demands and slammed Fujimori's "dictatorship" for "atrocious" jail conditions and the "physical and psychological" torture of imprisoned rebels.
The MRTA said it sought a "political and peaceful solution" to the crisis, but the government was dragging out the talks.
